articles.title: In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
articles.body:
In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

articles.title: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
articles.body:
Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

articles.title: Trump criticizes Ukraine's resumption of refinery strikes, calls Zelenskyy difficult negotiator – media
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump criticized Ukraine's decision to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries and described Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as a more difficult negotiating partner compared to Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, making the statement in an interview with Newsmax television channel on Thursday.
"Now, if you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace... there are many other targets to hit," Trump said.
According to the head of the White House, strikes on refineries producing diesel fuel harm the global energy market. Trump seeks to reduce energy prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, 2026, including through an agreement with Putin regarding the purchase of Russian diesel. Assessing the prospects of ending the war by the end of his term, the U.S. President expressed confidence that hostilities should end soon, but questioned the Ukrainian leader's readiness for compromises. According to Trump, negotiating with Zelenskyy is harder than with Putin, while mutual personal hostility between the two leaders presents an additional obstacle to a settlement.
Furthermore, the American president spoke in favor of holding elections in Ukraine, questioning the level of public support for the current government amid ongoing missile strikes on residential buildings. He also criticized his predecessor Joe Biden for providing Kyiv with multi-billion-dollar military aid and stated that the current administration is replenishing its own stockpiles of Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems and Tomahawk cruise missiles at record speed, after which Washington will permit allies to purchase these arms.
Separately, Trump reported that his administration is holding talks with Russia and China regarding the reduction of nuclear arsenals. According to his assessment, the U.S. ranks first in the world in nuclear capability, Russia second, while Beijing is currently less inclined toward denuclearization due to a lag that it could close within five to six years. The American president did not specify a timeframe for these negotiations.
On Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil infrastructure following a three-day pause that Kyiv agreed to after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed a drone attack on an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region, located approximately 290 km southeast of Moscow, where a fire broke out.
Previously, Ukraine fully agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's proposal for an energy truce and did not attack any energy facilities in Russia in response to their strikes.

articles.title: Human Judgement Is the Most Powerful Technology in the AI Age
articles.body:
In Ukraine, a Russian drone guided by artificial intelligence killed three civilians at a gas station, including a 19-year-old university student. In Gaza, an AI-assisted intelligence tool helped Israeli forces locate a Hamas commander. The subsequent airstrike killed him and, according to independent estimates, at least 125 other people.
Different wars. Different circumstances. But a deeply troubling question: As machines become more involved in decisions of life and death, are we losing sight of the human beings whose lives hang in the balance?
That question brought me back this month to a small white house in Reykjavík, Iceland.
Forty years ago, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met at Höfði House, representing rival nuclear superpowers divided by decades of distrust. They left without an agreement. Yet their willingness to talk, listen, and imagine what had seemed impossible helped lay the groundwork for historic nuclear arms reductions.
I remember that moment vividly. I was a young Icelandic exchange student living in the United States, watching two world leaders meet in my small home country. I could never have imagined that 40 years later, as President of Iceland, I would return to that same house to ask a new generation of leaders to find the courage to talk.
The enduring lesson of Reykjavík is not simply about nuclear weapons or diplomacy. It is about the extraordinary power of human connection and dialogue. And we urgently need to remember it.
Never have we possessed more sophisticated tools to communicate, yet our ability to understand one another seems increasingly fragile. We are connected across continents in milliseconds, but too often separated by fear, anger, and mistrust.
Our technologies can transform medicine, education, and human prosperity. Yet they can also accelerate conflict, undermine democracy, and challenge human control.
Crucial questions for the AI age
Thanks to new technologies like AI, our power has grown exponentially. But has our wisdom kept pace?
Over the past week, Iceland has explored that question not only through another conventional summit, but through a journey from remembrance to dialogue, and from dialogue to responsibility.
We began with a traveling exhibition from the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the testimony of a survivor of the atomic bombing. More than 80 years later, she still vividly recalls what she describes as the sudden appearance of a thousand suns, followed by unimaginable destruction, decades of devastating illness, and the stigma endured by survivors. No discussion of nuclear deterrence should ever lose sight of the human lives behind those words.
We then confronted the promises and dangers of artificial intelligence with technology experts, including Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin. The central question was not simply what AI can do, but what we should allow it to do—and who gets to decide.
Perhaps the most important conversations, however, happened far from the conference halls.
Across Iceland, young people invited fellow citizens to put down their phones and sit together to discuss the future they want to create. Students, parents, grandparents, teachers, and neighbors talked about education, belonging, technology, nature, and peace.
The young people were not asking adults to arrive with all the answers. They wanted to be heard. To be taken seriously. To have a voice in decisions that will shape their lives long after today's leaders have left office.
They understood something we too often forget: decisions made far from the people they affect are rarely wise ones.
I found that both humbling and hopeful.
Because dialogue is more than exchanging opinions. At its best, it is an act of recognition: I see you. Your experience matters. Your future matters. Even when we disagree, we share responsibility for what comes next.
The demands of dialogue
The purpose of dialogue is not always consensus. It is connection. And connection is where trust begins. Without trust, even the most brilliant solutions struggle to take root.
We carried that spirit back to Höfði House, where leaders from politics, technology, science, business, and civil society gathered to ask what responsible leadership demands of us today.
The result was A Call from Reykjavík, signed by three women presidents and open to others who wish to join. It calls for meaningful human control over powerful technologies, insists that decisions about war and nuclear weapons remain firmly in human hands, and places peace and responsibility to future generations at the heart of leadership.
The following day, in a public conversation moderated by renowned journalist Christiane Amanpour, President Nataša Pirc Musar of Slovenia, former Irish President Mary Robinson and I reflected on the choices before humanity.
Forty years after two powerful men met in Reykjavík, three women—indeed, three world leaders—came together to continue the conversation. Not because women have all the answers. We do not. But because progress requires more voices, more perspectives, and a willingness to listen across differences. And because the future must never belong only to those who currently hold power.
I do not believe dialogue is a soft alternative to leadership. I believe it is one of its most demanding forms.
It takes courage to listen to someone with whom we profoundly disagree. Humility to acknowledge what we do not know. And strength to resist reducing complex human challenges to slogans, enemies, or simple answers.
Dialogue does not mean abandoning our values, excusing aggression, or accepting injustice. Nor is it a substitute for action. It is how we begin to build the trust and understanding that make lasting action possible.
AI-assisted warfare
The wars in Ukraine and Gaza remind us of the devastating human cost of conflict. AI-assisted warfare adds another dimension: the danger of placing ever greater distance between those making decisions and those living with their consequences.
We must not surrender human judgment, accountability, or conscience to machines.
But technology alone is not the problem, and technology alone cannot provide the answer. We also need stronger human infrastructure: relationships, institutions, shared values, and habits of cooperation that allow us to respond collectively to danger.
We must equip the next generation not only with technical skills, but with the deeply human capacities to shape our future: listening, critical thinking, empathy, courage, and collaboration. In an age of intelligent machines, these may be our most essential skills.
Iceland is a small nation. We cannot dictate the course of global affairs. But perhaps our size reminds us of something larger nations sometimes forget: no one can build a peaceful future alone.
Forty years ago, Reykjavík showed that even the deepest divisions need not determine our destiny. Today, we need a new Reykjavík moment. Not one confined to a single house, summit, or handful of world leaders.
We need it in parliaments and boardrooms, classrooms and communities, across generations and between nations in conflict. Wherever fear has replaced curiosity, wherever people have stopped listening, wherever power has outrun wisdom.
The world does not lack intelligence, information, or ambition. What we too often lack is the courage to truly connect.
Of course, dialogue alone will not save us. But without it, I struggle to see how we can save ourselves.
The future will not be shaped only by the power of our technology or our weapons, but by the quality of our conversations—and the courage of the choices that follow.
Fortunately, we still have time. And we still have each other.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Starlink speed restrictions hamper Ukraine’s military, humanitarian operations
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that the Starlink system had not been completely switched off in Ukraine, but speed restrictions affected the country's ability to use it for certain military and humanitarian purposes.
Speaking at a briefing on the sidelines of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelesnkyy said the Defense Ministry remained in contact with partners and that he received indications from the White House that services would be fully restored.
He claimed Ukraine was not using Starlink to conduct deep-strikes against targets inside Russia, but relied on the system to operate interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
He said the restrictions also affected Ukraine's ability to carry out medium-range strikes against military targets.
Starlink-enabled drones, he said, were used to deliver food and water to Ukrainian personnel in positions exposed to enemy drone attacks.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine receives information from the US specifically about Russian ballistic missile launches, while dozens of countries also share intelligence with Kyiv.
He said Ukraine receives PAC-2 and PAC-3 air defense missiles from the US through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, with European countries financing the deliveries.
“So it's no gift. It's not for free,” he said, acknowledging that Ukraine is not currently a priority destination for the missiles, as many are being sent to the Middle East.
The Ukrainian leader criticized the recent US-Russia diesel deal and the prospect of lifting sanctions, saying Kyiv had not been informed in advance.
Ukraine, he said, proposed an energy ceasefire and offered the US to provide Kyiv with anti-ballistic missiles to protect energy infrastructure for the duration of the arrangement. “Don't give too many. Give us for the period you'll need for the duration of the diesel deal. I have not received that,” he said.
Responding to Donald Trump’s remark that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said negotiating with the US president was easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
He said ending the war remained his priority but accused Putin of showing no genuine desire for negotiations. He warned that concessions on sanctions could eventually lead to broader agreements with Moscow, including in the energy, chemical industry and banking sectors.
“In my view, we cannot perceive diesel deals, these arrangements. We cannot accept them because then there will be gas agreements. I'm sure of that,” he said.
Zelenskyy also rejected the notion that the war was solely about control of the Donbas region, saying Ukraine’s national existence was at stake. “The issue is not withdrawing from Donbas. It's the issue of our country's existence,” he said, arguing that Moscow’s objectives of the war extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
He said European countries understood the risks posed by Russia, and urged partners to continue supporting Kyiv.

articles.title: From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
articles.body:
From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has a powerful missile legacy; however, after the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of the industry's production capabilities and technological potential was lost. Modern developments are paving the way for the restoration of Ukraine's own ballistic missile capabilities.
For decades, Ukraine lost defense enterprises, technologies, and engineers, even though after the collapse of the Soviet Union it inherited a powerful missile industry. Now, amid a full-scale war, the country is trying to restore these capabilities. UNN, together with experts, examined why Ukraine lost part of its industrial potential and how difficult it is now to rebuild its own missile school.
Two years to develop a ballistic missile
After decades of decline in Ukraine’s defense industry, the country developed its own FP-7 ballistic missile in a short period of time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced its first combat use on October 1, 2026.
According to its CEO, Iryna Terekh, Fire Point created the missile in just two years.
When it comes to the development timeline for what one might call a conventional ballistic missile, it generally takes around 15 years on average, although it can range from 7 to 30. Before the FP-7, the shortest recorded development time for a ballistic missile was 7 years, whereas we reduced it to two
She said that the team worked intensively, sought to optimize the development process, and move to testing as quickly as possible. Some solutions had to be invented anew.
The CEO of Fire Point also noted that the company financed the development with its own funds.
The development of the FP-7 in two years shows that Ukrainian companies are capable of rapidly creating complex missile technologies even amid a full-scale war. It is now important to build on this result: establish serial production and continue developing the technologies.
But why does Ukraine have to restore its missile industry amid a war at all, if it once had a powerful industrial base and participated in the creation of strategic missile systems?
What Ukraine inherited after the collapse of the USSR
After the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine inherited part of the Soviet defense industry. The country had design schools, production facilities, engineers, and experience working on complex technological projects.
At the same time, military experts note that the inherited industry was not fully autonomous. According to defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, Ukraine received "fragments of broken production chains without a closed cycle and a specific pool of customers"—mostly authoritarian countries in the Third World, while no one even attempted to integrate into the U.S. or European markets.
After gaining independence, Ukraine needed to restructure this system to meet its own needs, determine priorities for developing the army, and create conditions for modernizing enterprises. However, for decades the defense industry did not receive sufficiently consistent support, while a significant part of state policy focused on using resources that were already available.
Military expert Ivan Stupak believes that Soviet stockpiles largely created a false sense of adequacy.
Until 2013, there was a department for surplus property, which was simply sold off. I knew people who worked at "Ukrspetsexport," and they told me: "We sold a tank to Pakistan, sold a plane somewhere else—everything is fine, we are making money." And these huge stockpiles created the illusion that we did not need to do anything
According to him, the country had technical developments that it could have used to advance its own missile programs, but it failed to do so in time.
How selling off assets turned into the loss of technologies
The problem was not only that Ukraine failed to create enough new weapons. The production capabilities themselves gradually weakened: enterprises lost orders, equipment became outdated, cooperative ties collapsed, and skilled workers left the industry.
Defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi attributes this to the lack of a long-term defense strategy and the state’s inability to restructure the inherited industry for new conditions.
In his assessment, some enterprises found themselves in a situation where they had to maintain production without stable orders or clear development prospects. This led to bankruptcies, the loss of equipment, and a reduction in technological capabilities.
The main problem of those twenty years was the absolute absence of a state defense doctrine. Instead of modernization and a transition to domestic production cycles, the country lived in an infantile illusion of security under the umbrella of the Budapest Memorandum, selling off Soviet arsenals for pennies and sincerely believing that it would never again need an army or defense industry
One of the most difficult consequences was the loss of specialists. Engineering expertise is developed through years of practical work, and without stable production, young specialists have no opportunity to gain experience and learn from their senior colleagues.
Money can buy any five-axis machine tool or build a clean hangar, but it is impossible to instantly restore the culture of chemistry, materials science, and solid-state physics. Over these two decades, we completely destroyed specialty chemicals and propellant production: the Shostka giants ("Zirka" and "Svema") deteriorated to such an extent that the country lost the complete production cycle for creating nitrocellulose, artillery propellants, and solid rocket fuel—something that cannot be restored without decades of chemical schools. We completely buried our own military microelectronics and microwave technology (ultra-high frequencies): plants such as Lviv's "Polaron," Kyiv's "Saturn," and Zaporizhzhia's "Gamma" no longer grew crystals or produced componentry for radars and active radar homing heads, which left us dependent on imports even for basic sensors. This was compounded by the degradation of specialty metallurgy: the loss of technologies for precision casting of monolithic blades for aircraft and gas-turbine engines, as well as special armor-grade and heat-resistant titanium alloys
According to him, another consequence was the loss of schools of large-scale engineering design.
Mykolaiv's heavy shipbuilding disappeared forever: along with the bankruptcy of the Black Sea Shipyard and the Shipyard named after the 61st Communist, the school of calculating and welding ocean-class hulls, aligning shaft lines, and coordinating thousands of suppliers for cruisers and aircraft carriers also died. Aircraft manufacturing at Kharkiv's KhAZ and Kyiv's "Aviant" lost the culture of serial assembly: one may have the brilliant Antonov design bureau, but if a plant produces one aircraft in ten years, engineers forget how to organize a serial takt-time assembly line
He emphasized that this concerns not only equipment and infrastructure, but also the experience passed from one generation of engineers to the next.
The main irreparable loss is "shop-floor memory." If the chief metallurgist or optical-mechanical alignment technologist at the Arsenal plant retires without passing the nuances on to an apprentice, the technology dies forever. And it is impossible to train a chief designer of a missile system or a developer of a thermal-imaging array with money—you need 15–20 years of continuous practical work on actual serial products for that
How to develop Ukrainian missile manufacturing
Restoring lost production capabilities is very difficult. Experts note that this requires not only engineering solutions, but also stable funding, long-term state orders, specialist training, and a clear strategy for developing the defense industry.
Military expert Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the full-scale war has forced Ukraine to accelerate weapons development. However, speed must not replace a systematic approach: defense technologies require long-term investment, and the result cannot always be achieved within a single budget year.
The defense industry does not work in such a way that you provide money today and go to a store tomorrow to buy a missile. You can invest in 2026 and see the result only in 2032
In his opinion, Ukraine needs a mechanism to support promising military developments modeled on the American DARPA agency, which funds research and development in defense technologies.
We have a great many talented people who can create extraordinarily interesting things. The main thing is to provide them with funding and ensure its stability
At the same time, Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi believes that restoring Ukraine's defense industry depends not only on financing individual enterprises but also on changing state policy. In his opinion, Ukraine needs to move from situational decisions to a long-term strategy that would provide for the development of private defense companies, the localization of critical components, and cooperation with European and American manufacturers.
True independence is not only a final break with moscow, but also a rejection of the role of an eternal supplicant with an outstretched hand before Western partners. We need our own agency: an aggressive focus on private defense tech, a rigorous review of the ineffective state sector, rapid localization of critical components, and parity-based integration into European and American production chains as an equal partner hardened by a major war
Fire Point could become one example of such development. Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, suggests that the company could become the foundation for further development of Ukraine's missile program and the creation of an entire family of ballistic missiles. He noted that the company is gradually expanding its areas of work—from drones and cruise missiles to ballistic weapons.
International cooperation could play a special role. Anton Zemlyanyi notes that Fire Point's plans to establish joint ventures with European manufacturers could help scale up production, attract partners, and reduce the risks of Russian strikes on production facilities. In the future, this could also open up new opportunities for integrating Ukrainian developments into European defense programs.
However, in the analyst's opinion, Ukraine should not build its missile program around a single manufacturer alone.
I would also not rule out other manufacturers, including state-owned ones. It is in Ukraine's interests to have several capable producers of missile weapons rather than depend exclusively on a single private company. This would create a broader production base, strengthen competition, and reduce risks for the missile program as a whole
Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the main lesson of previous decades is the need to invest continuously in one's own defense industry rather than remember it only when the country finds itself facing a large-scale military threat.
If you do not finance your own army, you will then have to stand for a year asking other countries for help. And there may not be another opportunity to do so

articles.title: Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
Ukraine has completely exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot air defence systems.
Source: The Washington Post, citing two Ukrainian officials and a NATO representative
Details: According to one source, Ukraine had only 10 Patriot missiles left as of 7 October.
"These were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining," a Ukrainian official said.
Quote: "A second person familiar with Ukraine's deteriorating air defence situation said the country is out of the sophisticated weapons, which are critical to shooting down incoming Russian ballistic missiles."
Details: A Ukrainian official stressed that "the situation is extremely tense".
CNN reported earlier that Ukraine had run out of Patriot missiles. According to its source, the shortage of ammunition was the reason Ukrainian air defences had been unable to intercept Russian ballistic targets during the latest large-scale attack.
Global missile stocks have been rapidly depleted by the war in the Middle East, launched by US President Donald Trump. In the first month of the war with Iran alone, the US used more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
Washington has made accelerating production a priority, but manufacturing a single missile can take up to 36 months.
Until now, missiles for Ukraine have been supplied through the PURL programme The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine , under which European countries pay for US-made weapons.
A senior NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the programme remained operational and that "air defence munitions like Patriot interceptors continue to flow".
However, a Ukrainian official raised concerns about the nature of the deliveries.
"Since May, supplies have been irregular, and right now no one can say with any certainty or guarantee that a delivery will actually arrive," the official said.
Background:
- Throughout the summer and autumn of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly urged Ukraine's partners to urgently increase supplies of missiles for Patriot air defence systems. In August, he stressed that Ukraine needed between 300 and 360 Patriot missiles to get through the winter safely. Meanwhile, Western deliveries had fallen sharply, from 675 missiles in 2023 to 364 in 2025, with only 264 planned for 2026.
- Meanwhile, according to reports in the media, the governments of Greece and Spain would rather keep Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service lives in storage than transfer them to Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges EU not to ease sanctions against Russia during leaders' meeting
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged the EU not to ease sanctions against Russia, stressing the need for a “strong” 22nd sanctions package from the 27-member union.
Speaking on the second day of an EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy accused his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin of seeking to “drag out” the Ukraine war into next year, saying Europe must be ready for this.
“I urge you not to ease sanctions against Russia or anyone linked to it. Putin uses every trick he can find to get money for making more weapons,” Zelenskyy said, noting Ukraine has warned that sanctions relief will result in others taking advantage.
The Ukrainian leader argued that the diesel deal between the US and Russia will never be enough to offset the impact of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz on global markets, but will rather “put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He stressed the need for a strong 22nd EU sanctions package, particularly calling for sanctions against all involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems and drones.
Zelenskyy said the financial cost of the ongoing conflict for Ukraine will be €155 billion next year and it needs at least €70 billion more for spending, including in terms of defense purchases.
He stressed the need to deal with Russian frozen assets, as well as called on European leaders to use every opportunity to strengthen air defense, emphasizing the need for a winter package consisting of 300 Patriot interceptors against Russian ballistic missiles.
“We are grateful that the EU is moving toward us. Four EU accession clusters have already been opened this year. And we need to open the remaining two by the end of the year. We are ready,” Zelenskyy said, calling on the union to keep Ukraine and Moldova's membership processes tied together.
Defining unity in Europe as a target for Russia, Zelenskyy said that in spite of disagreements and their differences, all of them seek a security system in Europe that “really works and can deal with today’s threats.”
“So, as we work now to finally stop Putin, to stop his war, we are doing this not just for Ukraine alone. We are working for security guarantees for all of Europe. For guarantees that this war will not be passed down to our children,” he said.
He expressed gratitude to those supporting Ukraine and those trying to keep Europe and the US together. “Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear -- either he chooses peace, or he gets no more money for his war,” he said.
Zelenskyy arrived in Brussels on Thursday to attend the European Council summit and hold a number of talks on the sidelines of the event.
Zelenskyy met with the presidents of the European Council and European Commission, as well as held talks with the Hungarian, Finnish and Swedish prime ministers on Friday.
On Thursday, he met his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Belgian King Philippe, and the prime ministers of Belgium, Denmark, and Poland.

articles.title: Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
articles.body:
Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
Russia expects to force Ukraine to capitulate this coming winter by disabling its energy system, particularly by leaving Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa without electricity, heat, or water, The New York Times reported. The newspaper reviewed a Russian government plan that Ukraine intercepted and showed to its European allies in September.
According to the plan, Russia would need about 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones, and 150 guided aerial bombs to cut off water, electricity, and heat to Ukraine’s three largest cities. Russian military planners believe a month of strikes at that intensity would destroy Ukraine’s energy system.
With the war now in its fifth year, previous attacks have left Ukrainian power plants unable to operate at full capacity, and each new strike quickly knocks them offline, the newspaper reported. Before the war, for example, the three combined heat and power plants supplying Kyiv had a total generating capacity of about 1.3 gigawatts. That has now fallen to about 500 megawatts.
If Russia’s plan succeeds, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa could lose 90% of their power generating capacity and see heat supplies cut by 90%, disrupting water and sewage systems, according to the newspaper.
Russia’s confidence that the plan can work stems largely from Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, particularly Patriot interceptor missiles, without which Ukrainian forces are virtually unable to defend against ballistic missiles.
Analysts agree that Moscow now has a better chance of succeeding in its air campaign than at any other point in the war. Ukraine’s missile defenses have been depleted by cuts in American aid, Russia’s missile and drone arsenal has grown more powerful and effective, and years of strikes have left Ukraine’s energy infrastructure far more vulnerable.
This makes Moscow extremely unlikely to agree to any version of the energy ceasefire Kyiv has repeatedly proposed. “The only card they have to pressure the Ukrainians are these air attacks. They don’t have anything else,” Harry Nedelcu, a director at the consulting firm Rasmussen Global, told The New York Times.
But history shows that such bombing campaigns, which devastate economies and civilian life, usually fail to force an enemy to surrender, the newspaper reported. The United States failed to achieve its aims this way in Vietnam, during the Persian Gulf War in the early 1990s, and in the current war against Iran.
“Punishing the adversaries’ civilian population and trying to break its will has a very poor historical track record for coercing it to concede defeat,” Seth Jones, a military expert at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, told the newspaper.

articles.title: Kiev out of Patriot interceptors – CNN
articles.body:
Kiev out of Patriot interceptors – CNN
Ukraine has exhausted its remaining US-made Patriot interceptor missiles used to defend against Russian strikes, CNN reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter.
The reported shortage comes amid a public feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky over Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.
According to CNN, the Ukrainian Air Force said it had intercepted four Russian ballistic missiles, apparently using the last of its remaining Patriot interceptors.
“Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles,” a source told the network.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in the hopes of lowering energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections in November. Trump defended the move as beneficial to consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda.
When asked about Zelensky’s criticism of the diesel deal, Trump suggested that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Zelensky, whose five-year presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to call new elections, citing martial law and the need for a months-long ceasefire with Russia. The Kremlin has argued that Ukraine would use a prolonged truce to replenish its armed forces and said it was only prepared to suspend strikes on election day.
Earlier this week, Zelensky said he would defy Trump’s demands to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which the US president blamed for high energy prices. Zelensky said Ukraine would agree to an energy truce only if Russia did the same. Moscow, however, said it was seeking a comprehensive peace deal on its terms rather than an unconditional ceasefire, which it argued Ukraine would exploit to its advantage.
The Trump-Zelensky rift deepened further this week after Ukraine reported sudden disruptions to Starlink and Starshield, satellite services provided by SpaceX that Kiev uses for drone strikes.
Ukrainian officials also said they had received no advance warning from their Western partners of Russian missile strikes on Kiev on two consecutive nights, Monday and Tuesday.
According to US media reports, American officials attributed the failure to detect the missile launches to bad weather, an explanation their Ukrainian counterparts reportedly found difficult to believe.
Zelensky renewed his plea for additional Patriot interceptors on Wednesday, urging the US and other partners “not to turn a blind eye to reality” and “to respond forcefully.”
The US, however, depleted much of its interceptor missile stockpile during the war with Iran, as widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that US stockpiles were virtually unlimited.

articles.title: White House ordered limits on Ukraine’s military satellite service — Reuters. Who made the decision remains unclear
articles.body:
White House officials instructed Pentagon leaders to limit Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service used by Ukrainian forces, Reuters reported on 15 October, citing three officials. The report came a day after a senior US official told Axios the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink restrictions.
Ukrainian forces rely on US-controlled satellite technology for battlefield operations and for intercepting Russian drones aimed at Ukrainian cities, so the latest restrictions have raised questions about how reliably they can depend on it.
Senior US official denies president requested restrictions
Asked about the order, a senior US official replied, “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Ukrainian officials contacted the White House, State Department and Pentagon on 13 and 14 October and were told it was a White House decision
European allies question Starlink restrictions
European officials raised concerns about the restrictions. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticized the throttling and said Ukraine must continue to receive full support, Spiegel reported on 15 October. Wadephul said Germany had questions for the US, noting that Germany finances part of the Starlink technology used in Ukraine.
On 16 October, UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that Starlink was back up and running, the Guardian reported. However, a Ukrainian Defense Ministry source said that military-grade terminals were working in motion again, but only at speeds of up to 160 km/h.
New data-speed restrictions disrupted drone missions
The military Starshield package previously had no data-speed restrictions, Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps told Novynarnia. Ukrainian officials said that after the restrictions were imposed, terminals disconnected when drones exceeded 160 km/h and sometimes at 80 km/h.
The Corps also reported 10–20-second connection drops at 110–120 km/h on the Huliaipole front, which made drones harder to control. One unit had to cancel some missions.
The restrictions came as US President Donald Trump pressed Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming them for soaring energy prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Ukraine suspects SpaceX imposed the restrictions to pressure Kyiv over the refinery strikes, but that motive has not been confirmed.

articles.title: Zelensky imposes refinery deal demand – WSJ
articles.body:
Zelensky imposes refinery deal demand – WSJ
Vladimir Zelensky is open to stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries for 100 days in exchange for a 300 km extension of Starlink satellite internet service coverage for the Ukrainian military, the Wall Street Journal has said.
The report comes as US President Donald Trump has ramped pressure on Zelensky to end the strikes, which he blames for surging global energy prices. In his interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump called Ukraine’s actions “a disgrace.”
In an article published the same day, the WSJ said that Republican Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer brought the deal to the Ukrainian leader during their visit to Kiev last Friday. The outlet claimed that it was told by unnamed sources that Zelensky had agreed to the proposal.
The extended Starlink coverage should help Ukraine target missile launchers inside Russia, according to the report.
Kiev, which is experiencing an acute shortage of US-supplied Patriot air defense missiles, has been struggling to contain Russia’s large-scale missile and drone strikes against military-related infrastructure across Ukraine. Moscow says the raids are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on civilian targets in Russia, including energy facilities.
The Ukrainians, who have relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones, have been “terrified” by the slowdown of satellite internet provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company this week, the WSJ said.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when UAVs flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. According to Reuters, the order to slow down the service came directly from the White House. Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink’s speed has increased over the last couple of days, but the restrictions haven’t been fully lifted yet.
Earlier this week, Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it kept ignoring Trump’s demands to cease energy strikes inside Russia. Officials in Kiev also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Russia was unaware of the Starlink slowdown for the Ukrainians, noting that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.”
Last month, Peskov warned that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.”
The American authorities apparently don’t require consent from Musk to expand the coverage of Starlink’s military component, known as Starshield, for Ukraine. The SpaceX CEO said earlier this week that its systems “are owned and controlled” by the US government, with the Pentagon and the US president deciding on the limits on their speed or usage.
On Sunday, Musk backed Trump’s suggestion that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” In a comment to a White House video with the US president’s criticism of the Ukrainian leader, the entrepreneur said that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
Zelensky reportedly wanted to personally discuss the expansion of Starlink coverage with Musk during his US visit to Washington in July, but the SpaceX CEO turned down the meeting.

articles.title: Poland provided secret military aid to Ukraine, Zelenskyy hints amid air defense shortages
articles.body:
Ukraine has received undisclosed assistance from Poland as it struggles to defend against increasingly intense Russian drone and missile attacks, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hinted during a meeting with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Brussels on 15 October, Radio Svoboda reported.
Ukraine’s air defense needs are greater than at any point since 2022, as intensified Russian drone and missile attacks strain existing systems and expose shortages of interceptor missiles. With US support increasingly uncertain amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington, European military aid is becoming more critical to Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and infrastructure.
Zelenskyy thanked Warsaw for its support, suggesting that some assistance had to remain confidential. He also specifically mentioned 20 mm ammunition, which Ukraine needs to defend its cities against Russian attacks.
“Sometimes this has to stay between the two of us,” Zelenskyy said, thanking Tusk for the aid.
European support increasingly important amid US rift
Ukraine is facing mounting pressure on its air defenses as Russia increases the scale of its aerial attacks. Ukrainian forces are also struggling with shortages of interceptor missiles, particularly Patriot missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic strikes, leaving the country vulnerable to further attacks.
The need for additional support comes amid growing uncertainty over US assistance under President Donald Trump. Washington has taken steps that have strained ties with Kyiv, including easing some restrictions on Russian fuel and pressing for an energy ceasefire that Ukraine says Russia has continued to violate.
Recent disruptions to US-linked intelligence and satellite support have also raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to detect and counter Russian attacks.
As uncertainty over Washington's role grows, European military assistance is becoming increasingly important for Ukraine's defense.

Defense cooperation continues despite political tensions
Tusk reaffirmed Poland's commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying Kyiv could count on Poland and the European Union. He also opposed easing EU sanctions against Russia, arguing that Europe should not take steps that help Moscow finance its war.
The meeting also came amid strained relations between Kyiv and Warsaw over historical disputes. However, Poland's government has maintained that these disagreements should not undermine military support for Ukraine, whose ability to resist Russian aggression is closely tied to Poland's own security.

articles.title: Trump calls Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries a 'disgrace'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has sharply criticised Ukraine for resuming attacks on Russian oil refineries, calling the strikes a "disgrace", as reports emerged that the White House had ordered restrictions on a satellite communications system essential to Ukrainian military operations.
According to a Reuters report, citing two US officials and a Western official familiar with the matter, the instruction to limit Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield service originated inside the White House.

The order was communicated to senior Pentagon officials, although the sources did not identify who authorised it.
Starshield, a military-grade satellite network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX, supports Ukrainian battlefield communications and drone operations. Ukrainian officials reported this week that satellite receivers installed on fast-moving equipment had stopped functioning, disrupting drone strikes against Russian positions and operations to intercept incoming Russian drones.
A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told Reuters on Thursday that the receivers had resumed working while moving, but only at speeds below 160 kilometres per hour.
A senior US official denied that Trump had personally requested the restrictions. The White House did not clarify whether another administration official had issued the order.
The disruption comes amid mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with Newsmax aired Thursday, Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of contributing to rising global fuel prices by targeting Russian refineries.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said, arguing that attacks on diesel production facilities threatened supplies needed by the United States and other countries.
Trump also renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy, saying he considered the Ukrainian leader more difficult to negotiate with than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine resumed refinery strikes on Thursday following a three-day pause intended to accommodate Trump's calls for an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy ended the suspension after Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite a ceasefire announcement made unilaterally by the US president.
The breakdown followed Washington's controversial agreement with Moscow to ease sanctions in exchange for additional Russian diesel supplies. Under the arrangement, Russia is expected to release more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel onto US and international markets.
Zelenskyy has criticised the deal, warning that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's continuing invasion. Some US lawmakers have raised similar concerns.
According to sources cited by the The Financial Times, Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons procurement arrangements unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries.
European leaders have meanwhile reaffirmed their support for Ukraine. Following talks with Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron said France remained committed to helping Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and protecting its civilian population and infrastructure.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also posted a message following discussions with European leaders in Brussels. Addressing Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian people in a post on X, Tusk declared: "YOU ARE NOT ALONE".

articles.title: What Is Starshield, SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink, and Why Is It So Important to Ukraine?
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces said Wednesday its battlefield efforts had been hampered overnight after losing some access to SpaceX’s military-grade satellite Internet service, which has become a lifeline as Kyiv weathers Moscow's attacks.
Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has recently been used by Ukrainian forces to strengthen its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military technology expert who advises Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed on the "military package" of Starshield services, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. “Our defense forces have not received any warnings about this restriction,” he said. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” He did not offer further details.
Tensions are high between the U.S. and Ukraine, as Zelensky has been vocal in his disapproval of U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import diesel from Russia, despite previous sanctions prohibiting it. The move has also caused a split in Trump’s own party, with several Republican lawmakers urging him to reverse course. After making the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine—but Zelensky swiftly accused Moscow of violating any such agreement and Ukraine has, in turn, resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace" in an interview that aired Thursday.
Speaking from the U.K., Zelensky said Wednesday it was a “pity” Ukrainian forces had experienced “difficulties” with Starlink services and intelligence, adding that he was surprised by the developments in Ukraine’s partnership with the U.S. In an interview on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelensky suggested he believed Starlink had been slowed down to damage him, and warned “people will die, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful.” He said he hoped the restriction was only a “mistake,” suggesting it was perhaps "a huge technical problem” at SpaceX.
However, in another interview, Zelensky said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will.”
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk addressed the matter, insisting that Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”
Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, later reported that the decision came from inside the White House.
TIME has reached out to the White House for further comment.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian national news agency Ukrinform reported Thursday, citing sources within the Ministry of Defense, that the Starshield service had resumed. TIME has reached out to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense for comment.
The discourse has raised questions about what Starshield is and how uniquely important it has become on the Ukrainian battlefield.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a program developed by Musk’s SpaceX that draws on the satellite and launch capability behind Starlink, its commercial satellite Internet network, to support national security operations.
According to SpaceX, Starshield is designed for government use, with an initial focus on three areas: Earth observation, communications, and hosted payloads.
“Starlink is basic interconnectivity, it's like the Internet. Starshield essentially grows out of the experience of Starlink,” Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King’s College London, tells TIME.
But the military value of that connectivity extends far beyond access to the Internet, Hilborne adds.
“In and of itself, satellite communications are not military technology, but it enables the military to communicate and amass a real-time, multi-domain picture of the battlefield, which some argue nobody else actually has at this stage,” he says.
Both systems also offer high-speed connectivity because of the satellite technology underpinning them.
“Starlink and Starshield are low on the Earth’s orbit, and they have a very high bandwidth, so lots of information can pass through those satellites, with virtually no delay on the signal,” Hilborne says.
There are more than 10,000 satellites in the Starlink network, while Hilborne says Starshield uses “a much smaller number of satellites.” However, the exact number of satellites associated with Starshield remains unknown, with experts telling TIME that such details are closely guarded due to national security considerations.
“They keep the contracting details on these things classified,” says Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
SpaceX, on its website, says Starshield is “designed to support U.S. National Defense use cases for the Department of Defense and other government partners.”
How is Starshield different from Starlink?
While both systems rely on closely related satellite technology, they differ in the services they provide and how they are intended to be used.
“Starshield refers to military services that actually operate through Starlink,” Harrison explains, comparing the services to “two different brands of a cell phone provider, even though your phone calls are going through the same towers.”
Starshield offers additional capabilities designed for military operations, including more advanced encryption and satellite imaging, experts tell TIME.
“It's got another extra set of capabilities over and above Starlink,” Hilborne says. “They use some of the same technologies, but it would be highly encrypted, and they have different sensors that allow them to image what they call ‘Earth observation.’ That can give a radar imaging of the Earth [which] has advantages over optical pictures.”
Yet experts say the distinction between the two systems is not always clear, particularly given how closely their underlying technology and operations are connected.
How important is Starshield for Ukraine?
Starshield and the satellite communications technology underpinning it have become vital to Ukraine’s military operations against Russia.
Hilborne describes the technology as “highly critical” to Ukraine, explaining that any restrictions could cut communications with military equipment traveling above that speed, leaving operators without the information needed to guide their missions, as once that speed threshold is exceeded, the connection “suddenly cuts off and it's flying blind,” he says.
The consequences are particularly serious for Ukrainian drone operations, which rely on communications for both strikes against Russian targets and defensive missions against incoming attacks.
“It's really critical for drones, both the offensive medium range strikes, but also affects Ukraine's ability to fly defensive drones against the incoming Russian drones,” says Hilborne.
Beyond its role in drone missions, experts say satellite communications also offer important advantages over other forms of battlefield connectivity.
Harrison notes that “the big benefit of using satellite-based communications is that you can communicate over longer distances in a variety of terrain, and it does have some jam-resistant features to overcome electronic forms of attack.”

articles.title: Belgium to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by year-end – PM De Wever
articles.body:
Belgium plans to transfer ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, Prime Minister Bart De Wever announced after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, according to The Brussels Times, citing a statement from the prime minister.
"We will deliver 10 this year," De Wever said, explaining that delays in the delivery of F-35 fighter jets had affected the timeline for transferring the Belgian F-16s to Ukraine, but that the new aircraft are already beginning to arrive.
According to the prime minister, the fighter jets will help Ukraine defend itself against Russian drones. He emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs combat-ready aircraft and confirmed Belgium's readiness to make its contribution.
Belgium delayed the transfer of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine due to the postponement of the delivery of American F-35s, which are intended to replace the aging aircraft. During a meeting with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Prime Minister De Wever also discussed the supply of Belgian-made ammunition for the F-16s and reaffirmed the need for continued financial support for Ukraine from the European Union.
"I made it clear that, as far as I am concerned, the European Union must continue to support Ukraine. I have a clear view of how this can be done. I have not yet discussed it, but I think it will come up tomorrow and I am prepared for that," he said.
As reported on Thursday, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy was granted an audience with King Philippe of Belgium, during which the president emphasized the importance of supporting Ukraine and its air defense system, as well as supplying Ukraine with F-16 fighter jets. Prior to this, Zelenskyy held a series of meetings with representatives from NATO, Poland, and France.

articles.title: Russia Builds Massive Jet Drone Launch Base Near Ukraine in Just Six Weeks
articles.body:
Russia has nearly completed a massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in its southwestern Rostov region in just six weeks, satellite imagery analyzed by Reuters shows, as Moscow ramps up attacks that are increasingly difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
The facility near Millerovo, roughly 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles) from a Russian air base, has grown from an empty field into a complex covering about 0.9 square kilometers (0.3 square miles) – roughly the size of 126 soccer pitches – between Aug. 31 and Oct. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense experts say the site is designed to launch Russia’s latest jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (373 miles per hour).
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, identified eight launch platforms along the facility’s western edge. Two already had launch rails installed, according to Reuters’ analysis of satellite imagery.
The base could be operational within weeks, if not sooner, Monnik said.
“The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” he said.
Russia ramps up faster drone attacks
The construction comes as Russia sharply increases its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the hardest-hit areas.
Russian use of the faster drones increased roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data.
White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
Unlike slower, piston-powered drones, jet-powered models are harder to stop with relatively inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukraine has increasingly relied on to counter Russian attacks.
With the full-scale war in its fifth year, Ukraine expects Russia to intensify drone and missile strikes this winter, putting additional pressure on its air defenses.
The new facility could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones in 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational requirements, Monnik said. Russia typically launches its drones in smaller waves throughout the day.
New base could be harder for Ukraine to hit
The new site is located close to Millerovo air base, home to Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
DroneSec assessed that the launch facility likely falls within the air-defense coverage of the military air base, potentially making it more difficult for Ukraine to strike.
The rapid expansion of Russia’s drone-launch infrastructure also poses a potential challenge for NATO countries, which face growing concerns over Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.

UK Sends More Storm Shadow Missiles to Ukraine to Disrupt Russian Attacks Before Winter
The United Kingdom is sending Ukraine additional long-range Storm Shadow cruise missiles to disrupt Russian military operations targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter, according to Bloomberg on October 15.
The additional deliveries were discussed during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to London on October 14, when he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Bloomberg cited people familiar with the matter who requested anonymity because the weapons shipment has not been publicly announced.

The UK has not disclosed how many missiles are being transferred or when they will arrive. British officials consider Ukrainian strikes against Russian military facilities involved in attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure to be defensive operations, the sources noted.
The sources also indicated that London opposes restricting Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia while Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian territory. The position contrasts with Washington’s reported pressure on Kyiv to suspend drone strikes against Russian oil refineries, the outlet added.
The UK government declined to comment on the reported shipment. Britain has not disclosed the total number of Storm Shadow missiles supplied to Ukraine since 2023 and does not routinely announce individual deliveries, Bloomberg noted.
Manufactured by European defense company MBDA, Storm Shadow missiles have a range exceeding 250 kilometers and use terrain-hugging flight profiles to penetrate enemy air defenses. Ukraine first deployed the British-supplied missiles against military targets inside Russia in November 2024.
Alongside the long-range strike capability, Britain is also strengthening Ukraine's air defenses ahead of winter. London has committed $2.12 billion to supply more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles over four years, a weapon effective against the jet-powered drones Russia increasingly uses in deep strikes.
A further $59.7 million in surface-to-air missile deliveries was announced alongside Zelenskyy's visit, with $13.3 million accelerated to meet Ukraine's most urgent winter air-defense needs. Britain is also pressing partners to tighten sanctions and adopt a ban on maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas exports.
