articles.title: Russia pushes its drone war into Volyn Oblast on NATO border, cutting power to 370,000 as strikes creep toward EU
articles.body:
Russia is pushing its drone war westward, into a Ukrainian region that borders NATO. Russian drones attacked Volyn Oblast through the night of 16 October, hitting civilian and critical infrastructure and leaving 370,000 subscribers without power, regional administration head Roman Romaniuk says. Volyn borders Poland, a NATO member, and Belarus, a Russian ally.
Russia’s jet-powered drones keep flying farther west, and now the strikes reach deeper into the center and the EU-facing frontier too. Moscow launched more than 850 Shahed drones at Ukraine in about a day and a half, including a record roughly 360 on the central Kirovohrad Oblast, precisely as a speed cap on Starlink degraded the interceptor drones Ukraine’s air defense relies on.
Moscow escalates its attacks after winning sanctions relief from the diesel deal of US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin and sensing pressure on Ukraine, exploiting the moment its defenses were artificially restricted.
“Russia takes advantage of every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does,” Zelenskyy says, noting the skies had not been clear for a single hour.
A night that turned deadly in the west
In Volyn Oblast, the damage was concrete and lethal. Debris fell on a power line in the central Lutsk community, cutting electricity and disrupting water supply, and the city lost power entirely with public transport halted, Lutsk council secretary Andrii Razumovskyi says.
The heaviest toll came in Manevychi, where a drone hit the private enterprise Agrofrukt LTD, killing one person and injuring eight. By 10:46 AM, the fire there was contained, and residents were asked to seal windows, doors, and vents due to the risk of an ammonia release from a damaged facility.
A capital-to-border map of the same assault
Throughout the day, Russia has struck Kyiv and its region, and the Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Rivne, Kharkiv and Donetsk regions, along with Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Poltava and Ivano-Frankivsk.
By reaching western border regions at once, Russia is widening the pressure on civilians across the country and edging closer to the EU.

articles.title: Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemen presidential palace
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden
The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
The attack hit command centres located inside the presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.
Government military sources in Yemen said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in Thursday's strikes on Aden's Al-Maashiq palace in the divided country's south.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani had been present at the time, but "was not harmed in any way".
The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them".
Yemen's civil war - in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 - reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.
Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," said Dr. Rayed Krimly.
The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.
Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired "several ballistic missiles" at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
Oman meeting refused
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.
Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times this month.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
He added the group had "worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors", saying they now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
(AFP)

articles.title: Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is ‘disgrace’, Trump says

AI generated
WASHINGTON – European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit on Oct 16 as US President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”.
The EU is hosting Zelensky in Brussels at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Trump blindsided Zelensky last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
The US has also struck a diesel deal with Russia, angering Ukraine and European allies.
“We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don’t see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter,” Zelensky said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.
“The winter package is not only energy, it’s also air defence and funding.”
In the latest attacks, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for 2027.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
“We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs.
“Because always, at the start (and) at the end of every conversation, people need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting... for us.”
No ready-made European alternative to Starlink
Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used by Kyiv for battlefield communications and drone operations.
A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Oct 15 that Starshield receptors were only working at speeds of up to 160kmh, complicating their use for military missions.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” said the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
“We are working on the new sanctions package to put the pressure on Russia, and we of course hope that we do this with all our partners around the world.”
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Oct 15.
Zelensky told Reuters earlier in October that Ukraine had agreed a plan with European partners that would allow it to close a US$27 billion (S$34.5 billion) deficit in its military spending for 2026, allowing it to order the drones needed to continue fighting at the start of 2027.
However, Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said recently Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap for 2027 of US$32.6 billion – and that does not include an estimated US$40 billion in direct military supplies from allies.
“I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine,” said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
Sounding a more sceptical note, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker urged caution in the debate over making new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.
“There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from. I’m surprised too,” he said. REUTERS

articles.title: 22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of 22 House lawmakers is urging President Donald Trump to fully implement the new Russia sanctions law and revoke a license allowing certain Russian diesel transactions. In a letter sent on 15 October, they copied Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and requested details on planned sanctions, tariffs and waivers.
Their request comes as the law’s first requirements fall due on 18 October, while lawmakers from both parties challengethe administration’s decision to allow certain Russian diesel transactions. Some restrictions take effect automatically, while others require presidential action. The law does not specify a penalty for the president missing the deadline.
What the Russia sanctions law requires
Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by votes of 86–11 in the Senate and 262–159 in the House. Trump signed it on 18 September. Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina, died in July.
Restrictions taking effect automatically on 18 October include a ban on US banks and broker-dealers processing transfers to or from the Russian government, a ban on new US investment in Russia, a ban on new US investment in Russia’s energy sector, and a ban on US energy exports to Russia.
Other measures require presidential action by the same date. The law directs Trump to review and sanction Russian officials, oligarchs and shadow-fleet vessels, sanction the Bank of Russia, specified Russian banks and state-owned companies, and impose tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods. Tariffs of up to 100% can apply to goods from countries among the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas, or among the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.
Trump may waive sanctions, restrictions and tariffs under the law if he first certifies in writing to Congress that a waiver is in the US national interest and submits a report explaining its basis.
The diesel license at the center of the dispute
House members also urged Trump to revoke General License 135, which the Treasury Department issued on 9 October and that is valid until 7 April 2027. It permits certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States. Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets and predicted prices would fall sharply, according to a 9 October Truth Social post.
On 13 October, a bipartisan group of 12 senators also urged Trump to rescind the deal and revoke the license. Seven senators said the deal conflicted with a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports.
The Graham Act says nothing in its provisions affects the Treasury secretary’s existing authority to issue general licenses. That provision does not resolve whether the diesel license complies with the separate 2022 law.
A White House official told Newsweek the administration would comply with the Graham Act. Bessent said the administration would use “all the legal authorities we have” and called the deal “good for the American people,” Fox News reported on 11 October.
How the sanctions could be lifted
Separately, the law sets a process for terminating sanctions, restrictions or duties against Russia. Trump must report to Congress that Russia has signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine’s government and ceased military hostilities against Ukraine, as well as activities to overthrow, dismantle or subvert its government. Congress has 30 days to block termination through a joint resolution of disapproval, or 60 days for reports submitted between 10 July and 7 September.

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
articles.body:
Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
Ukraine was unable to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones to protect civilians because Starlink connection speeds had been reduced.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking after meetings on the sidelines of the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October, as reported by European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels
Details: Zelenskyy added that the reduction in Starlink speeds had also prevented Ukraine from striking military targets in occupied territories and delivering water and food to Ukrainian troops.
He also stressed that the Armed Forces of Ukraine do not use Starlink to conduct long-range strikes on Russian territory.
"We use [Starlink] to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families. We use specialised interceptors that move at high speeds. Interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out that Starlink had not been switched off, but its connection speed had been reduced.
Quote: "When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds… In other words, we were unable to use a tool to protect civilians. This is very painful and unpleasant."
Details: The president explained that jet-powered Shaheds fly at speeds of more than 400 km/h, while the Starlink restrictions had reduced the equipment speed available to Ukrainian troops intercepting Russian drones to 70 km/h.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine uses Starlink for mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in temporarily occupied territories, but the reduction in connection speeds had prevented it from carrying out those operations as well.
In addition, Starlink is needed to deliver water and food to Ukrainian troops who spend weeks or months on the front line in areas under the Russians' full drone surveillance.
Zelenskyy noted that the Defence Ministry is in daily contact with the United States and had recently received information that the connection speed had been resumed.
"If that is the case, we are very grateful," the president added.
"We approached SpaceX and the White House to ask them to enable this capability," Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine has not received a positive response to its request.
Background:
- Reuters previously reported that the order to restrict the use of the Starshield satellite system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone control, had come from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation and report back to Congress on the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- Axios previously reported that Trump's administration supposedly had nothing to do with the incident. Washington attempted to shift responsibility to SpaceX, saying the White House does not control the company's actions.
- Zelenskyy publicly described the communications restrictions as a mistake that would lead to casualties and destruction.

articles.title: Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
articles.body:
Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN – In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
Mahdi Zolfaghari is an Associate Professor at the Department of Asian Studies in Allameh Tabataba’i University

articles.title: ‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
articles.body:
‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.

articles.title: Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland
articles.body:
Donald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.
Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered an on-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.
Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found that an essential piece of kit – a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and, as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”
Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week, Ukraine endured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.
All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing to buy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make a splash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just as Russia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in the US invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meeting at one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.
In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleague Luke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?
Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination of greed, ideology, dictator envy and kompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as “aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than “151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend brought credible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executives of key European defence firms.
What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.
For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.
All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new book War is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.
The best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.
- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
- US midterms: Trump, war and America’s future

Russia’s Air Surveillance Takes a Hit as Ukraine Strikes $100 Million Nebo-U Radar
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Nebo-U long-range radar station in Krasnodar Krai overnight, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 16.
The strike targeted a 55Zh6U Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri in Russia’s Krasnodar Region during the night of October 16. A fire broke out near the facility following the attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Nebo-U is a three-dimensional VHF-band radar designed to detect and track aircraft, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. The General Staff estimated the system’s value at approximately $100 million.
“Strikes on such systems reduce the enemy’s ability to control airspace and promptly detect aerial targets,” the General Staff stated.
Ukraine’s military did not disclose the weapons used in the strike or provide an assessment of the radar’s condition after the attack. It noted that operations against key Russian military facilities are continuing.
The strike follows earlier Ukrainian attacks on the same type of radar as part of an effort to blind Russia's air surveillance network.
On August 27, Ukrainian drones hit a Nebo-U station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia's Rostov region, roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, from the front line.
The airfield serves as a launch point for Shahed-type attack drones and other strike and decoy UAVs used against Ukraine's eastern, central, and northern regions. That attack formed part of a broader campaign to establish sustained fire control over the site.

articles.title: Belgium promises to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by end of year
articles.body:
Belgium promises to transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by end of year
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has stated that the country will transfer 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
Source: Anadolu Agency
Quote from De Wever: "We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine."
Details: During a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the EU summit, De Wever and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed Ukraine's military needs.
He also emphasised that Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets, calling the F-16s one of the few weapons capable of effectively defending against "Russian jet-powered drones."
De Wever also reported that during the meeting with Zelenskyy, they discussed the possibility of supplying ammunition for the F-16s, including rounds manufactured by the Belgian defence company FN Herstal.
It is noted that the leaders also discussed Ukraine's financial needs. At the same time, De Wever did not specify whether this concerned the use of frozen Russian assets, the majority of which are held in the Belgian depository Euroclear. Belgium had previously opposed using these assets to finance a reparations loan for Ukraine due to potential legal and financial risks.
Background:
- It was previously reported that Ukraine had agreed with Belgium on the accelerated transfer of three F-16 fighter jets by the end of 2026. This was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

articles.title: Belgium to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, says premier
articles.body:
Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year to help strengthen its defense capabilities, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Thursday.
Speaking at a press conference following the first day of an EU summit in Brussels, De Wever said he discussed Ukraine's military needs with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit.
"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," De Wever said.
He stressed that Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets, describing F-16s as among the few weapons capable of effectively defending against "Russian jet-powered drones."
De Wever added that the two leaders also discussed the possibility of Belgium supplying ammunition for the F-16s, including some manufactured by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.
The leaders also discussed Ukraine's funding needs, although De Wever did not elaborate on the possibility of using frozen Russian assets held largely at Belgian-based Euroclear to support Ukraine.
Belgium previously opposed a proposal to use the frozen assets to finance a reparations loan for Ukraine, citing potential legal and financial risks.

articles.title: Russian drones kill three in Ukraine, cut power to 1 million as US, Russia seek further cooperation
articles.body:
Russian drones killed at least three people across Ukraine early on Friday, hit two shopping centers and temporarily knocked out power to over 1 million people nationwide after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.
A 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man died, and 12 more people were wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. He had earlier put the death toll at three.
Ukraine's energy ministry said its repair crews had restored power to over 1 million people who lost it in Russian attacks on Friday. It was unclear how many people were still without power.
Almost 300,000 remain temporarily without power
In the northwestern region of Volyn, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Governor Roman Romaniuk. He said 370,000 people were temporarily without power in the morning, although 100,000 of them got supply back later on.
The blackout could last for at least 24 hours in Volyn's regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said on Facebook.
Romaniuk said that drone attacks continued throughout the day, striking a customs terminal and torching about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, which sits on a major trunk road from Kyiv to Poland.
Other attacks hit at least two shopping centers, one in the northern city of Sumy, which sits close to the front line, and one in the neighboring region of Rivne, officials said, the latest in a spate of Russian assaults on malls and markets.
Pictures from emergency services in Sumy showed blood spattered across the floor and shots of the center's damaged entrance.
Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping center and other sites in Rivne, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.
Ukraine's energy ministry said large parts of the city of Rivne and the surrounding area were without power after attacks on energy infrastructure there.
Russia, US to announce new joint initiatives beyond diesel deal
Russia and the United States will soon announce new joint initiatives beyond a recently agreed diesel deal, President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Friday.
Dmitriev said the two countries were discussing joint data center projects, including facilities that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
Dmitriev said that the projects would be launched before the end of what Moscow calls its "special military operation" in Ukraine.
Following a report in the Financial Times that the US had proposed European countries transfer some frozen Russian assets to a vehicle overseen by Washington to try to revive stalled peace talks, Zelensky said that Ukraine could not risk any deal being struck to return the assets to Moscow.
Ukrainians struggling with a fifth year of Russian attacks on their power grid and other civilian infrastructure have said they are appalled by Trump's decision to open the US market for Russian diesel. They have also condemned his attempts to blame fuel shortages caused by the Iran war on Kyiv's military strikes on Russian refineries.
"In my view, we cannot accept these diesel deals, these agreements, because gas deals will follow. I am absolutely certain of this. Sanctions will be lifted on other things as well after gas," Zelensky told reporters in Brussels.

articles.title: Belgium promises to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year
articles.body:
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said at a press conference attended by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
“Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets and we can make our contribution,” De Wever said following a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the European Council meeting in Brussels.
"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," the prime minister said. As Belgium is modernizing its air force with U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets, the country said it would transfer some of its F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine.
On Sept. 29, Zelensky said that Belgium will provide Ukraine with three U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets by the end of the year.
De Wever said that Ukraine urgently needed the fighter jets, as they were one of the weapons capable of defending Ukraine from "Russian jet-powered drones."
The Geran-5 jet-powered drone is Russia's latest attempt to force Ukraine to capitulate. Small, and with a tubular fuselage reminiscent of a missile rather than a drone, the Geran-5 flies higher, faster, and is significantly more difficult to shoot down. Russia's jet drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Zelensky and De Wever also discussed the possibility of supplying Ukraine with ammunition for the F-16s.
F-16s are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used for intercepting Russian missiles and drones during aerial strikes against Ukraine. They can also be deployed to launch missiles at Russian positions along the front line.

articles.title: SCALP, AASM Hammer, and Aster 30: France Has Granted Ukraine All the Promised Licenses
articles.body:
Ukraine has received all the licenses France promised for the domestic production of three types of weapons: Aster 30 air defense missiles, AASMHammer guided bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the development.
In July, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the licensing agreement following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The agreement allows Ukraine to produce these weapons domestically under French licenses.
Ukrainian forces have been successfully employing Aster 30 missiles for an extended period as part of the SAMP/T surface-to-air missile systems supplied by France and Italy.
The modern Aster 30 Block 1 variant can engage aerodynamic targets, including aircraft, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), at ranges of up to 120 km and altitudes of up to 25 km.
In addition, the system can intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 30 km.
The French AASM Hammer is a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided Western-designed bombs into precision-guided munitions.
Unlike the American JDAM, AASM Hammer kits are equipped with an integrated rocket motor, enabling them to engage targets at ranges of up to 15 km when released from low altitudes and up to 70 km when released from high altitudes.
Currently, two versions are available: the Hammer 250, designed for 227 kg Mk 82 bombs, and the Hammer 1000, designed for 908 kg Mk 84 bombs. Both are available with different guidance systems.
The Franco-British SCALP EG / Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile measuring 5.1 metres in length, weighing 1,300 kg, and equipped with a 450 kg warhead designed to destroy hardened, fixed targets.
The missile was developed by Matra and British Aerospace beginning in the late 1990s. It has been in service with France and the United Kingdom since 2003 and is manufactured by the MBDA consortium.
The French SCALP-EG and British Storm Shadow variants are essentially identical in design, differing primarily in their software and the specifics of their integration with carrier aircraft.

articles.title: AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
articles.body:
AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
TEHRAN— Hossein Taeb, head of Iran’s Basij Organization, says the use of artificial intelligence in defense and intelligence operations has improved the accuracy of target identification and precision strikes, highlighting the technology’s growing role in Iran’s military capabilities.
Speaking on Thursday at the first Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Conference in the southeastern city of Kerman, Taeb said AI had strengthened intelligence gathering and target assessment, adding that its applications had extended to the naval and aerospace divisions of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) and other branches of the armed forces.
Taeb also discussed 'the objectives of the US-Israeli war against Iran,' arguing that attacks on military commanders, scientists and air-defense systems were intended to weaken the country’s defenses and undermine the scientific foundations of its development.
Protecting Iran’s scientific capabilities
Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

articles.title: “We Are Not the Number One Priority”: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Faces Severe Patriot Missile Shortage
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
“We Are Not the Number One Priority”: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Faces Severe Patriot Missile Shortage
Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its US-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, most available supplies of these missiles have been directed to the Middle East for an extended period.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“There is currently a severe shortage. Most PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles have been going to the Middle East for quite some time. This is no secret,” Zelenskyy said.
“We are not the number one priority when it comes to the allocation of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. Nevertheless, we are grateful for the number of missiles we can receive through PURL,” he added.
Despite the limited availability, Ukraine continues to receive some Patriot interceptors from the United States through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. The program allows European partners to finance the purchase of US-made military equipment for Ukraine.
“We receive PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from the United States through the PURL program. Europe pays for them, meaning these are not free missiles or gifts,” Zelenskyy explained.
The Ukrainian president expressed gratitude to NATO, European countries financing the purchases, the White House administration, and the United States for their continued involvement in supplying air defense equipment.
With interceptor missiles remaining in short supply, Kyiv is also working with international partners to secure additional deliveries in smaller quantities.
“We are working with Europe and other countries around the world, gathering 2, 5, or 10 missiles at a time. However many we can agree on, however many of the necessary missiles we can obtain, that is how many we deliver to Ukraine to protect people,” Zelenskyy said.
The president emphasized that strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses remains particularly urgent as Russian attacks continue to threaten critical infrastructure across the country.
“Today, we are protecting infrastructure, primarily the energy sector. You are well aware of all these challenges,” Zelenskyy stated.
His remarks follow reports of an even more critical situation involving Ukraine’s Patriot missile stockpiles, with a source familiar with the matter telling CNN on October 15 that the country had completely exhausted its available interceptors.
According to the report, the shortage has significantly undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the country’s vulnerability to further attacks.
The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

articles.title: Romania finally holds Russia responsible for the drone attacks on ships off its coast, and wants a joint NATO command for the Black Sea
articles.body:
Romania has proposed a joint NATO military command for the Black Sea, as drones hit four merchant ships in 24 hours, three of them off its coast, and its foreign minister said Russia "bears full responsibility." NATO ambassadors will discuss the attacks next week.
Russia’s strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea have escalated this autumn and reached NATO shores. Drones have attacked at least eight merchant vessels near Romania and Bulgaria since 5 October, two of them inside Romania’s territorial waters. Until now, neither country had named the attacker, and Bulgaria still says it cannot prove who it was. Romania’s patience appears to have run out, and next week’s NATO meeting will show whether the alliance is ready to go further as Russia’s war spills beyond Ukraine’s borders.
Acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță wrote on Facebook on 14 October that "the Black Sea needs a joint military command of the NATO riparian states." "The Black Sea incidents, involving drones, sunk ships, and naval mines, oblige us to act, not wait," he wrote, after a call with his Bulgarian counterpart. Leadership and location would rotate among the member states. Romania is ready to host the command on its coast from 2028 and would accept a start on Türkiye's coast until then, he said. He proposed that Romania and Bulgaria send NATO a joint letter backing the idea.
The next day, Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu wrote on X that four commercial ships had been attacked over the previous day, including in Romania's territorial waters and exclusive economic zone, and that eight people had died. "Russia is turning the Black Sea into a dangerous area for civilian ships," she wrote. "Killing sailors from commercial ships, both in this region and anywhere in the world, is a crime. Russia bears full responsibility for these developments."
Earlier that day, as two tankers burned off Romania's coast, Bucharest had said it was still checking whether drones were involved.
Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks
Țoiu said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had agreed to convene the allies within days, after he met Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Brussels. NATO ambassadors will meet next week, France 24 reported. No date has been announced.
An escalating drone strike campaign
Drones have been hitting merchant ships for weeks on the route from Ukraine's Danube and Odesa ports to the Bosporus. Besides the latest strikes off Romania, Reuters counts at least five cargo ships hit near Romania and Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors dead or missing, most of them outside any NATO member's territorial waters. This week the strikes reached Romania's own waters.
- The Comoros-flagged tanker Yara J was hit inside Romanian territorial waters late on 14 October, off Sulina, the port at the mouth of the Danube. Its crew was unharmed, and it was towed to the Romanian port of Constanța.
- Early on 15 October drones struck the San Marino-flagged chemical tanker Wine Trader about a mile outside Romanian waters, also southeast of Sulina. Five of its 12 crew were rescued. Seven were still missing on 16 October, when rescuers returned to search the ship.
- Two more ships were also targeted, Reuters reported: the Marshall Islands-flagged Sea Destiny, inside Romanian waters according to NATO, and the Tanzania-flagged Dania J, moored at the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail.
Țoiu did not say which ships her eight dead were from, and Reuters still lists the Wine Trader's seven as missing. A NATO military source told Reuters the drones that hit both tankers came from Russia.
Romania's president says too early to say
Romania's president has not gone as far as his foreign minister. Dan told reporters in Brussels it was "obvious" that the attacks were Russian attempts to destabilize Romania and Bulgaria and reduce support for Ukraine. But he also said it was too early to say definitively that Russia had launched the drones, according to Politico.
Bulgaria, Romania's partner on the command proposal, says it suspects Russia but cannot prove it. Two ships were hit off its coast on 13 October, and one, the HS Dignity, sank. The other, the Chelsea 3, is Ukrainian-owned.
Radev told parliament on 14 October that the attacks worked in Russia's favor and that "logic leads there." "The problem is that we cannot prove it," he told MPs. Sofia summoned the Russian ambassador. Radev also said EU leaders would discuss a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea.
Bucharest has blamed Russia for drones before, though over its airspace, not its shipping. On 27 July it expelled a Russian diplomat after prosecutors confirmed that fragments of drones downed on Romanian territory were Russian. Russia, Romania's Foreign Ministry said then, "bears exclusive responsibility."
Ukraine ships most of its farm exports across the Black Sea. Euromaidan Press's David Axe has written on how the fight over shipping there has escalated.
Russia is losing the Black Sea grain war it started. Its answer is to sink civilian ships off Romania and Bulgaria

articles.title: Zelensky's ask: 300 Patriot missiles, 70 billion euros, and Russian assets
articles.body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky used his appearance at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels to list the main things Kyiv needs to survive the winter and beyond, but those asks won't come cheap.
"I am grateful for your support for Ukraine," Zelensky told EU leaders.
"Without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions Putin would have gone much further by now," Zelensky said.
But with Russia ramping up its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones to pummel Kyiv, and the U.S. taking steps to undermine Russia sanctions and Ukrainian security, Zelensky also came to the bloc with new requests for help.
read also
"We need a winter package... 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The U.S.-made Patriot are considered the only technology currently capable of consistently taking down Russian ballistic missiles, and several European countries still hold stocks of them, such as Spain and Greece.
But for Spain, European diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that there is a real fear that Madrid will not receive any more Patriot missiles in the future because of U.S. President Donald Trump's personal dislike for Spain's center-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
Greece on the other hand has a visceral fear that depleting its own supplies of Patriots might be perceived as a sign of weakness by neighboring Turkey, which Athens fears Ankara would act upon by annexing Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Likewise, Ukraine's demand to "deal with the frozen assets," unsettles several countries around the table.
Using the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the EU to support Ukraine came up in late 2025, but consensus on the idea was out of reach.
"We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war," Zelensky said.
Aside from the fears of holders of those assets, principally Belgium, about Russian retaliation for such a move, several European countries also fear that entering into such appropriations could fracture the global financial system, as countries move their wealth only into jurisdictions deemed friendly to them.
For Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, touching those assets remains very much a no-go.
"My personal view is that if you have immobilized assets, like in every war, even the Second World War, they were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there's always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever told journalists at a press conference during the night of Oct. 15.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier? ... Yes, there are ... Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," De Wever said.
And the risk of Russia's assets being returned, despite some wishful thinking from the U.S. that Europe would hand them over, is nonexistent. The EU bound itself in December 2025, so that any vote to unfreeze the Russian immobilized assets must be unanimous.
"Nobody could ever dream of operationalizing those immobilized assets without unanimity here around the table," De Wever said.
On top of requesting the Russian assets, Zelensky also asked the EU to fill Kyiv's budget hole for 2027.
"The war will cost 155 billion euros ($174.5 billion) next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion) more from you," Zelensky said.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he added.
But the request for 70 billion euros comes only six months after the bloc approved a 90 billion euro loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. The idea was always that third countries would step in to help bridge the remaining gap, but so far only Norway has done so.
And the government has been notoriously unclear at communicating its financial needs, as noted earlier that day by Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
However, Zelensky's estimate of a 70 billion euro shortfall does match the estimated shortfall figure that a senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's financial situation shared with the Kyiv Independent.
On all three requests, even if they land on sympathetic ears, a decision would still not be expected the same day.
And because there is nonetheless a European consensus to support Ukraine, the demands are very likely to dominate discussions in Brussels over the next weeks.

articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
Countries along NATO’s eastern flank are growing increasingly concerned about the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine.
Poland has scrambled its defences once again as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to Poland’s border.
Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded.
It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences.
During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured.
In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.
Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes.
In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region.
Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices.
Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations.
Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said.
Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters.
That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing.
Drones hit two ships off Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof.
Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and antidrone systems to bolster its defences.
“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Reuters news agency reported.
Stoyanov said he plans to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO antidrone initiative by the end of October.
Romania’s president has also said that his country has asked for additional equipment.

articles.title: Why Ethiopia and Eritrea’s march to war demands global attention
articles.body:
The distant thunder of drones over Adigrat is not merely another African conflict. It is the sound of a continent’s most fragile peace shattering—and with it, the already slender prospects for stability across the Red Sea corridor that carries twelve per cent of global trade. Barely eight years after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and President Isaias Afwerki embraced in Asmara, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s handshake now lies in ruins.
Eritrean troops have crossed into northern Tigray, advancing up to sixty kilometres into Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia has responded with multiple drone strikes targeting those forces, destroying lorries and ammunition, witnesses say, amid reports of civilian deaths. Both nations have severed diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia calls it an “all-out invasion.” Eritrea calls it an “unprovoked war of aggression.” The truth matters less than the trajectory: two of Africa’s most battle-hardened armies are edging toward a conflagration neither can afford, yet both seem convinced they cannot avoid.
The roots of this rupture are not mysterious. They are anchored in geography so cruel it functions as destiny. Ethiopia, home to 130 million people, is the world’s most populous landlocked nation. It depends on Djibouti for over 95 per cent of its maritime trade, paying between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in port fees—a haemorrhage equivalent to the cost of building a Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam every three years.
A nation that once commanded the Red Sea through the ancient port of Adulis now watches its commerce squeezed through a single corridor. This is not merely an economic inconvenience. It is a structural wound that successive Ethiopian leaders have described in existential terms.
Abiy’s response has been to demand sovereign maritime access—specifically, to the Eritrean port of Assab, barely sixty kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Eritrea, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year liberation struggle, views this as nothing less than a threat to its territorial integrity and the very meaning of its statehood. Asmara’s information minister has accused Ethiopia of openly working to bring about regime change by sheltering and supporting armed opposition groups. The result is a security dilemma of terrifying symmetry: each side’s defensive measures confirm the other’s worst fears.
Into this vacuum have stepped external powers with interests that have little to do with Ethiopian or Eritrean welfare. Israel has publicly endorsed Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions, with its ambassador describing support for the effort as “clear Israeli policy.”
The strategic logic is cold: a strong, allied Ethiopia provides a non-Arab anchor in a region where Israel seeks to counter Iranian and Houthi influence, and where its recognition of Somaliland has already signalled a willingness to redraw regional alignments. The United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia’s largest investor and a quiet supplier of military technology, forms the other pillar of this de facto axis.
The United States, by contrast, has intervened with uncharacteristic directness. On 14 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that “the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” demanding respect for sovereignty and an immediate halt to cross-border incursions. Washington has even lifted certain sanctions on Eritrea—a pragmatic pivot driven not by any moral reassessment but by the urgent need to secure Red Sea shipping lanes against Houthi attacks. This is containment dressed as diplomacy, and it carries an uncomfortable implication: accountability for Eritrea’s role in the Tigray war has been quietly subordinated to maritime security.
The regional picture is equally troubling. Egypt and Sudan have aligned themselves with Eritrea, driven by their own existential anxieties over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Cairo views the dam as a threat to its 97 per cent dependence on the Nile. Addis Ababa views it as a sovereign right.
The result is a “river-versus-sea” confrontation in which the Nile and the Red Sea have become inseparable theatres of competition. Ethiopia’s army chief has openly accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the very rebels now fighting federal forces.
The human cost of this geopolitical chess game is already being paid. The 2020–2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people. A renewed interstate conflict—this time involving heavy drone strikes, conventional armies, and the potential spillover onto Eritrea’s Red Sea coast—would create a humanitarian catastrophe of a different magnitude entirely. Millions of Ethiopians already face severe food insecurity.
The fragile Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray war has dissolved into renewed fighting across Amhara and Afar, with former allies now united in an armed alliance against the federal government. Ethiopia cannot fight a civil war and an interstate war simultaneously without fracturing.
Yet the most disturbing truth is that neither Washington’s pressure nor the African Union’s exhortations have altered the trajectory. The AU, headquartered in Addis Ababa, is structurally compromised—it cannot credibly mediate a conflict involving its host nation.
The Gulf states possess the financial leverage to broker a settlement, but the UAE’s deep ties to Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Egypt make a unified mediation unlikely. The window for diplomacy is closing, and it is closing fast.
What is required is not another communiqué. It is a recognition that Ethiopia’s landlocked status is not a moral failing to be corrected by force, but a structural reality that demands a structural solution. The path forward lies in negotiated maritime access frameworks, joint port management arrangements, and regional economic integration that makes war materially irrational.
Ethiopia’s accession to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System in October 2026 offered a glimpse of what patient, institutional cooperation could achieve. That glimpse is now being extinguished by the roar of drones.
The international community must act with a clarity that matches the urgency. The United States, the Gulf states, and the African Union must coordinate a single, unambiguous message: there is no military solution. But pressure alone is insufficient. The world’s strategic powers must offer Ethiopia a credible economic alternative—guaranteed, legally binding access to Red Sea ports under international law, backed by investment and infrastructure. Eritrea, for its part, must be assured that its sovereignty is not a bargaining chip.
The Horn of Africa has burned before. The world watched then, and the world did too little. It must not watch again. The drones over Adigrat are not a warning. They are a countdown.
