AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said on Oct 15 that Washington is holding talks with Moscow and Beijing aimed at denuclearising the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The US outpaces Russia on its number of deployed warheads.
During an interview with Newsmax, Trump said he expects China to “catch up” with the US within the next five years.
“The whole thing is a shame, because I’d love to denuclearise if possible, but we’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation,” Trump told the outlet.

articles.title: Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, news agency Reuters reported- citing four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
Reuters reports, citing a US military official, that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade.
Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

articles.title: US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
articles.body:
US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says.
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.
China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.
“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”
China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.
Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.
China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.
Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.
A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.
Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.
“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said

articles.title: EU fast-tracks merger of three European firms into one SpaceX rival. It wants to end reliance on US satellites that failed Ukraine this week
articles.body:
The EU plans to fast-track antitrust approval for Project Bromo, a satellite venture aimed at reducing Europe's reliance on American space technology, Bloomberg reports. The news comes amid the latest reports that the US administration has switched off Elon Musk's Starlink service to Ukrainian forces amid US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, according to Reuters.
Project Bromo would merge the satellite arms of Italy’s Leonardo and France’s Airbus and Thales into a single European player capable of competing with SpaceX and American and Chinese rivals.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has backed the project, Eunews reports.
“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” she said at an international space summit in Paris last month, citing Bromo by name.
A year of quiet groundwork before the filing
The partners have been preparing the ground for months. Over the past year, they discussed potential competition concerns with EU officials to resolve them before filing a formal application, according to Bloomberg. The companies have not yet applied, but Brussels expects them to do so in the coming weeks.
For large deals, regulators usually hold preliminary consultations to flag obstacles early. If the companies offer concessions, such as selling some assets, the deal could clear after a first-phase review of a little over a month. If competition concerns remain, the Commission could open an in-depth probe lasting several months.
The caveat behind the Starlink-rival label
The push is part of a wider European scramble for space autonomy. Ukraine is building a satellite system of its own beyond any single company’s control, and France recently poured 1.35 billion euros into the operator Eutelsat.
For Ukraine, such systems are indispensable, as Kyiv's operation against Russia's war capabilities relies on them.

articles.title: Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years after election: Report
The Trump administration is backing efforts to form a broad Israeli unity government after this month's election that could keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister for up to two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, according to an Israeli media report.
The proposal would exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and bring together Netanyahu's Likud party with Eisenkot's Yashar party, Israel Hayom reported on Friday.
The newspaper cited unnamed US and foreign political officials familiar with the discussions. Neither Washington nor the Israeli parties involved have publicly confirmed an agreed plan.
Israel is due to hold a Knesset election on 27 October.
Polls have suggested neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the fragmented opposition is guaranteed a stable governing majority, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations.
According to Israel Hayom, the US and regional governments believe a broad coalition would be better placed to make major decisions on ending regional conflicts and advancing President Donald Trump's wider Middle East agenda.
One unnamed foreign official quoted in the report said a fragile minority government would be unable to make the "major and decisive political decisions" the region required.
The proposed arrangement would allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister for up to two years before Eisenkot succeeded him, according to the report.
During that period, the government would be expected to work towards ending wars on multiple fronts and reaching political agreements with regional states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration has been pushing Riyadh to join the Abraham Accords and normalise relations with Israel.
Washington has linked that effort to other parts of the US-Saudi relationship, including F-35 fighter jets and a civilian nuclear programme.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said, however, that normalisation with Israel would require meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.
The issue has also become entangled with Washington's proposed nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Trump has said would depend on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords.
According to Israel Hayom, Saudi Arabia is also seeking a different political configuration in Israel before moving forward.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has recently met several senior Israeli politicians, including Eisenkot, the report said.
The contacts were said to have been handled carefully because of concerns over perceptions of US interference in the election.
But Israeli politicians were reportedly told that Washington and other governments would welcome a broad and stable coalition without far-right parties.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has emerged as one of Netanyahu's principal challengers in the election and leads the centrist Yashar party.
The proposed government would also seek to address domestic issues that have deeply divided Israeli politics.
These include demands for an official inquiry into the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, disputes over the judiciary and the continuing row over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has denied reports that he is directly involved in efforts to engineer a unity government.
He has nevertheless said he wants to avoid repeated elections and see a stable government formed after the vote.
The reported US effort comes as Israel's election remains highly fragmented, with Palestinian parties potentially playing a decisive role if neither major bloc secures a governing majority.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defenses down 114 out of 149 Russian drones launched at Ukraine overnight

articles.title: Zelenskyy’s warning that Russian airspace is becoming dangerous is proving true: Russia temporarily restricted operations at 27 airports amid a massive drone attack
articles.body:
Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at 27 Russian airports, Deutsche Welle reported on 16 October, citing its own calculations based on reports from Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines on 1 September that “Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe.” Overnight, most of the airspace over European Russia was closed.
By morning, more than 200 flights had been canceled or delayed at Moscow airports, Deutsche Welle reported, citing figures compiled by a Russian Telegram channel.
The list included airports in the capital. All four Moscow airports temporarily suspended arrivals and departures, the Russian outlet Astra reported on 16 October. Russian authorities said they had shot down dozens of drones, while flights were delayed and diverted to alternate airfields, according to the report.
Massive drone attack on Russia: 644 UAVs in one night, 94 shot down near Moscow
The temporary airport shutdowns were likely a consequence of a massive drone attack on Russia. From 8:00 p.m. on 15 October to 8:00 a.m. on 16 October, Russian air defenses allegedly intercepted and destroyed 644 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles across 26 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, according to Russia’s Defense Ministry.
According to the list of regions published by the Russian Defense Ministry, the drone attacks covered a vast area of Russia, from regions bordering Ukraine to the Moscow region, the Volga region, the country’s northwest and southern regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Russian air defenses shot down a total of 94 drones approaching Moscow over the evening of 15 October and overnight, according to calculations by the Russian outlet RBC Radio, citing statements by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
In the Kaluga region, air defenses destroyed 27 drones over the evening and night, the regional governor reported. At 9:27 a.m., he updated the figures, saying another 48 UAVs had been shot down overnight, bringing the total to 75. According to preliminary information, there were no casualties or infrastructure damage.
In the Tula region, air defenses allegedly destroyed a total of 32 Ukrainian drones. There were no casualties, according to regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev in his Telegram channel.
In the Vladimir region in western Russia, authorities repelled drone attacks overnight. In the city of Vladimir, a drone attempted to attack a heating infrastructure facility, but the attack was stopped, Vladimir Region Governor Alexander Avdeyev reported. Minor damage was reported, but there was no information about casualties.
Ukraine has not yet commented on its involvement in the attacks.
The practical consequences of canceled Russian flights
Passengers on flight SU6312 from Kaliningrad to Moscow were unable to land in Moscow because of airspace closure, so the aircraft was diverted to Nizhny Novgorod, Terravia reported. After landing, passengers remained on board for about two hours before being allowed to disembark at 3:30 a.m. Instead of continuing their journey to Moscow by air, they were supposed to be transported by bus, with the trip expected to take about seven hours, the outlet reported.
Passengers were not provided with food or drinks, and one woman could not find a seat on the bus, so she purchased a ticket for an early-morning train herself.
Since the beginning of the year, all four Moscow airports have been completely shut down simultaneously at least 19 times, the Russian outlet Agentstvo reported. During the first 14 days of October, the restrictions lasted 101 hours and 38 minutes, compared with 46 hours and 33 minutes in September, according to the report.

articles.title: Coercive diplomacy: What does the call between Netanyahu and al-Sharaa really mean?
articles.body:
The phone call between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Syrian interim leader Ahmed al-Sharaa—following months of firing salvos via fighter jets, missiles, and third-party intermediaries, alongside strikes that targeted the courtyard of the Syrian Ministry of Defence and the perimeter of the presidential palace—was no ordinary diplomatic formality. Rather, it was a condensed moment signalling a tectonic shift in the geopolitics and power balance of the Middle East.
When Netanyahu and Sharaa speak directly to discuss sectarian tensions in the Druze-majority province of Sweida, we are not merely witnessing a localised security arrangement dictated by geography and overwhelming force. We are standing before a series of uncomfortable questions shaping the region’s future: Is Syria capitulating entirely to the rhythm of Israeli power, which has established itself as an unyielding arbiter in the new Syrian landscape? Or is this a pragmatic response from Damascus to pressure from an Arab bloc seeking regional normalisation—a bloc that views any effort to rebuild and reintegrate Syria as passing, one way or another, through the neutralisation of active fronts with Tel Aviv?
Furthermore, who granted Israel and Netanyahu the political and international mandate to act as the self-appointed custodian over Syria’s Druze minority?
The most realistic answer lies elsewhere: in a devastated economy, a shattered state apparatus, and a transitional authority that has come to realise that rebuilding Syria requires, above all, zeroing out external hostilities. States emerging from the crucible of war do not enjoy the luxury of managing multiple conflicts at once. Today’s Syria looks far closer to this exhaustion model than to the legacy slogans of traditional “Resistance.”
Yet, the phone call poses far larger strategic dilemmas than it answers: Is this a tactical manoeuvring aimed at preventing escalation and buying time, or the beginning of a structural shift redefining Syria’s place on the regional map? Is Sharaa treating Israel as an unalterable geopolitical reality, or is the entire region entering an era where ideological mantras surrender to the imperatives of economic survival, reconstruction, and stability?
Anticipating an answer requires reading this new Syrian stance not as absolute surrender, but as a tightrope walk driven by a “survival mindset.”
Sharaa lacks the military capacity to engage an adversary that strikes the heart of Damascus with international impunity. Conversely, he understands that total compliance with Israeli terms risks sparking domestic fragmentation and delegitimising his rule regionally.
Hence, the most plausible regional scenario is Damascus moving toward ending the “active state of war” without entering the formal fold of political normalisation—establishing a security framework for borders and minorities that satisfies regional patrons while isolating Syria from radical axes to minimise reconstruction costs.
On the Israeli side, Netanyahu is attempting to engineer an advanced “politico-security belt” reaching deep into Syria’s social fabric.
By asserting proxy guardianship over minority populations like the Druze, Tel Aviv aims not only to secure its northern border, but to institutionalise a model of a “regional patron” holding the keys to stability in broken neighbouring states.
This style of power projection forces any future government in Damascus—whether led by Sharaa or another—to operate within a security architecture drafted in Tel Aviv long before it reaches the halls of the United Nations.
Ultimately, what transpired was not the announcement of a new alliance, but a mutual acknowledgment of a new balance of power. It is an equilibrium in which Netanyahu realizes his security influence remains incomplete without ordering his immediate Syrian backyard, while Sharaa recognizes that reclaiming statehood may require, for the first time in decades, managing relations with Israel through state pragmatism rather than ideological rhetoric.
The significance of the call lies not in its brief duration, but in its role as a barometer for a Middle East where yesterday’s political impossibilities have become today’s negotiating points.
Yet, all these calculations could swiftly evaporate or invert should Netanyahu lose power in the upcoming Israeli elections.
READ: Damascus rejects Israeli politicisation of Syria’s Druze after Netanyahu’s brief call with al-Sharaa
The core dilemma rests not solely within Syria, but in the nature of the Israel that Netanyahu embodies today. Under his tenure, Israel has transformed from a state seeking security-driven compromises into an actor behaving as the region’s absolute power, backed by an unprecedented surplus of self-confidence—perceived by its adversaries as military hubris and by its leadership as earned strategic dominance. Thus, any potential Syrian opening cannot be disentangled from the persona of the man wielding power in Tel Aviv.
Is Damascus reaching out to Israel as a permanent state institution, or is it coercively adapting to an extraordinary “Netanyahu moment” and the hard facts it has established on the ground? This question is no less vital than the issue of normalisation itself. If Netanyahu departs the political stage and Israel reverts to more conventional, less aggressive security calculus, the strategic weight of these contacts may shift overnight. They may well be reinterpreted as fleeting security arrangements dictated by temporary power dynamics rather than enduring strategic realignments.
When the dust settles, we may discover that the true historical event was not the phone conversation between Sharaa and Netanyahu, but the historical epoch that produced the phenomenon of Netanyahu itself—an era that compelled the entire region to redefine power, deterrence, and sovereignty under the weight of a prolonged war that has not yet ended, but will not forever remain governed by the logic of a victor who believes history moves by his will alone.

articles.title: U.S. Army’s Europe Typhon battery fires its first Tomahawk
articles.body:
- A U.S. Army Typhon battery assigned to Multi-Domain Command Europe fired its first Tomahawk at China Lake, California, on Sept. 28, 2026.
- It was the third Typhon launch in the continental United States, after soldiers completed five weeks of training with the U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin.
A newly fielded U.S. Army Typhon missile battery assigned to Europe has fired its first Tomahawk cruise missile, launching it during a live-fire at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake, California, on Sept. 28, 2026, in what the service said was the third Typhon launch within the continental United States.
The Mid-Range Capability Battery of 3rd Battalion, 12th Field Artillery Regiment, a long-range fires battalion under Multi-Domain Command Europe, carried out the launch. Typhon, built by Lockheed Martin, is a truck-mounted launcher that fires the Tomahawk Land Attack Missile and the SM-6, missiles originally developed for U.S. Navy warships, and it fills the gap between the U.S. Army’s shorter-range rocket and missile launchers and its long-range hypersonic weapon, letting ground commanders hit targets more than 1,600 km (1,000 miles) away with Tomahawk.
“We get that range for that combatant commander to give them options and capabilities where they really haven’t had it before from the land force,” said Lt. Col. Derek Bartlett, commander of 3-12 Field Artillery.
Bartlett said strikes at that range would previously have been requested from the joint force, typically from the U.S. Navy, and that “the Army now has that capability.” Before the launch, soldiers in the battery went through a five-week training program run by the U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin field service representatives to learn how to operate and maintain the system.
“They’re incredibly good at what they do now,” said Bartlett. “I’m very comfortable deploying them forward after these five weeks.”
The 3-12 battery is one of four Mid-Range Capability batteries the U.S. Army has created and falls under Multi-Domain Command Europe, which brings together the service’s land, air, sea, space and cyber capabilities to strike targets. According to the U.S. Army, the first battery was activated in January 2024, while the 3-12 battery was activated in November 2025.
“It requires all domains to work in unison for a kinetic strike to happen,” said Command Sgt. Maj. John Hespe, the battalion’s senior enlisted advisor.
“Rockets in the field artillery community are going to continue to evolve,” said Hespe. “It’s going to provide better options for commanders to choose to fire from land based emplacement in any country at any time.”
Typhon has already deployed outside the United States: a battery went to the Philippines in April 2024 for exercises, and the system was shown in Japan in 2025, moves that drew protests from China. In Europe, Washington and Berlin announced in July 2024 that the United States would begin episodic deployments of long-range fires to Germany in 2026, including Tomahawk and SM-6 missiles, which puts a Europe-based Typhon unit in line with those plans.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine has "plenty of targets" in Russia beyond oil refineries
articles.body:
Trump says Ukraine has "plenty of targets" in Russia beyond oil refineries

articles.title: Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
articles.body:
Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow has exposed divisions within the West over its anti-Russian stance, as the US shifts toward a more pragmatic approach, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl has said.
US President Donald Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, easing sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April 2027 in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. The move marks a departure from the Western sanctions policy imposed on Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
Speaking to TASS on Friday, Kneissl described the agreement as more than a “symbolic breakthrough,” pointing to the 300,000 tons of Russian diesel expected to reach the US and global markets by November.
“The EU says that this undermines the West’s united position. However, one could also say that this marks a shift by the US toward a more pragmatic approach, while the EU continues to pursue a purely ideological line,” she stated.
The agreement has drawn criticism from European leaders attending a two-day EU summit in Brussels this week. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused Trump of sidelining the bloc, telling reporters that “Trump, by doing that business with Putin, stabbed us in the back. We have to do something.”
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, however, welcomed the agreement, arguing that lower fuel prices were essential to Europe’s economic competitiveness. “Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate,” he said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the agreement as a “gift to Putin,” while defending Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed on Friday that the bloc would maintain its sanctions against Moscow despite Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
Brussels’ hardline stance contrasts with that of EU member Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian energy and has sought to maintain economic ties with Moscow. Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly called for diplomacy rather than continued military support for Kiev.
The dispute has also strained relations between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Vladimir Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for pushing up global fuel prices.
Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as a “weak decision” and accused Trump of “betrayal.” Ukraine continued targeting Russian energy facilities, including a refinery in Ryazan Region on Thursday, prompting Trump to condemn the attacks as a “disgrace.” At Friday’s summit, Zelensky sought additional financial and military assistance from European leaders but left empty-handed, with only renewed promises of support.
The confrontation comes as global diesel supplies remain under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, in an effort to ease shortages and bring down prices.

articles.title: Romanian Institutions Bought Banned Russian Cybersecurity Software
articles.body:
Reported by
More than 80 Romanian public institutions continued to purchase cybersecurity software from a Russian-founded company after the government explicitly banned its use over national security concerns, a review of public procurement records reveals.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania passed a 2022 law prohibiting public entities from acquiring cybersecurity software originating fromRussian individuals or entities. In March 2023, a government order officially blacklisted a broad range of products from Kaspersky, a Russian cybersecurity firm.
However, procurement data shows that between March 2023 and September 2026, 83 public institutions and authorities made 131 purchases of prohibited software.
In an emailed statement, Kaspersky said it “does not have any inappropriate ties to any government.”
“Kaspersky has maintained that the claims about alleged security risks that the company’s products might have and related restrictions are based on the current geopolitical climate rather than a technical analysis of Kaspersky software security,” the company said.
“To date, no party has presented any public evidence that the company’s products might pose a threat to corporate or private users,” Kaspersky added.
The Romanian buyers of Kaspersky software included hospitals, municipal governments, schools, and other public institutions.
Notably, less than two months after the blacklist was published, the National Institute for Laser, Plasma and Radiation Physics bought two-year Kaspersky antivirus licenses for three devices. According to its annual reports, the research institute generates classified information and works under contracts with the Ministry of National Defense, the "Ferdinand I" Military Technical Academy, and NATO.
“We would like to clarify that the purchased product has never been installed or actually used on any computer, server, or other IT system belonging to the institute,” the institute said in an emailed response to questions.
Sebastian Burduja, who headed Romania's Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digitalization when the rules were introduced, attributed the continued purchases to a lack of enforcement staff.
"On the other hand, as we all suspect, we likely have a pro-Russian strain within Romanian state institutions," said Burduja said, who is now a deputy in the country’s parliament.
Kaspersky is named after its founder, Eugene Kaspersky, a former software engineer for the Soviet Union Defense Ministry who studied mathematics at a school sponsored by state authorities like the KGB, the secret police and intelligence agency. From its founding in 1997, Kaspersky grew into one of the world's largest cybersecurity providers. But the company’s business has been hampered by international restrictions, including a 2024 action by several countries.
The U.S. prohibited the sale of many Kaspersky products, citing risks to national security. The company rejected the allegations, claiming the ban was based on the "geopolitical climate and theoretical concerns" rather than product integrity.
Germany, Lithuania, and Italy have also issued formal warnings or implemented measures to phase out the software from critical infrastructure.
Under Romanian law, violating the ban on Kaspersky products is an administrative offense carrying fines between 50,000 and 200,000 lei (between $10,500 and $42,000).

articles.title: Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
articles.body:
The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.
This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.
The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.
“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.
After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.
“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.
The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.
He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.
As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.
“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”
Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.
As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.

articles.title: Trump calls Zelensky ‘more difficult to deal with than Putin,’ says he’s ‘not a big fan’

Trump calls Zelensky ‘more difficult to deal with than Putin,’ says he’s ‘not a big fan’
U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with the right-wing channel Newsmax that he finds it harder to negotiate with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky than with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Trump said. “Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. He doesn’t want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t. No, I’m not a big fan of Zelensky.”
He again criticized Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he said are driving up global fuel prices. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets. … There are a lot of targets that you can hit,” Trump said.
Trump again raised the issue of elections in Ukraine, which have not been held because of martial law. He expressed doubt that Zelensky retains public support amid the ongoing war in Ukraine. “I think you need an election because there’s nobody that’s telling me that the people of Ukraine are satisfied having missiles hitting their apartment building,” he said.
Trump said he still believes the war will “end soon,” because “they actually both would like to see it end.” However, he said, there are certain difficulties. “Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin. And when you have that kind of hatred, it’s very hard to get something settled,” Trump said.
On October 9, Trump agreed with Vladimir Putin on supplies of Russian diesel fuel to the American and global markets. Ukraine and Europe criticized the decision.
On October 11, the U.S. president announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a truce in the energy sector. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the truce announced by Trump “came as news” to him. On October 15, Zelensky said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries for three days but would now resume strikes because Russia had not observed the truce. Russian authorities claim Ukraine never stopped its strikes.

articles.title: Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
articles.body:
Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives have written to President Donald Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Source: Congressman Jim Costa's website; Ukrainian journalist in Washington Ostap Yarysh on Facebook
Details: The letter was authored by House Foreign Affairs Committee member Jim Costa, together with the co-chairs of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus in the House of Representatives: Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson. The lawmakers stressed that the first mandatory deadline for the key sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to take effect expires on 18 October.
They emphasised the need to step up economic pressure on Moscow ahead of winter.
Quote: "As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war. Utilising the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously."
Details: In the letter, the lawmakers also expressed deep concern over the US Department of the Treasury's decision on 9 October to issue General Licence No. 135, which permits transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian diesel fuel into the US.
They called on the administration to immediately revoke this permit and prevent any new exemptions that restore the flow of petrodollars into the Kremlin's war chest.
Furthermore, the House members have asked the administration five questions and demanded written answers by 18 October. They want to know what steps will be taken to ensure the full implementation of all mandatory sanctions, tariffs and bans, and whether the White House intends to delay any provisions or grant exemptions to them.
The lawmakers are also calling for the administration to publish a list of Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies targeted by the restrictions and to clarify whether foreign banks and Russia's shadow fleet operators will also be affected. They are further demanding details of which countries will face secondary tariffs for purchasing Russian energy, what safeguards will be in place for allies, how pressure on Putin will be measured, and why sanctions are being eased despite the existing legislative ban on Russian energy imports.
Among the 22 signatories to the letter are leading representatives of both parties, including Republicans Michael McCaul, Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Democrats Steny Hoyer, Jim Costa, Marcy Kaptur, Josh Gottheimer and Dina Titus.
Background:
- On 17 September, the US Congress passed bill H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation authorises 500% tariffs on Russian goods, secondary tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, and mandatory sanctions against key sectors of the Russian economy.
- On 19 September, US President Donald Trump signed the Graham Act into law, setting the first 30-day deadline for the implementation of its provisions for 18 October.
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Donald Trump, calling the diesel deal with Moscow a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to immediately revoke the licence and move to full implementation of the Graham Act.

Ukraine’s air defenses down 253 Russian drones, nine Banderols during day
